questions.question: Define slope aspect and explain why north-facing slopes in South Africa are warmer than south-facing slopes, noting when and where the contrast is greatest.
questions.expected_answer: Aspect is the direction a slope faces. In the Southern Hemisphere the midday sun stands in the northern sky, so north-facing slopes receive rays at a high, concentrated angle and for more hours, while south-facing slopes receive glancing, diluted rays. The contrast is greatest in winter, when the sun is lowest, and in east-west valleys, where one wall faces due north and the other due south.

questions.question: Describe how katabatic drainage on a clear winter night produces a valley temperature inversion, and locate the thermal belt, frost pockets and radiation fog within the resulting structure.
questions.expected_answer: After sunset the slopes cool by radiation; air against them chills, becomes denser and drains downslope under gravity, ponding on the valley floor. The floor becomes the coldest zone with warmer air above — temperature increases with height, an inversion. The thermal belt is the warm, frost-free mid-slope zone above the cold pond; frost pockets form where ponded air in the floor or hollows falls below zero; radiation fog forms when the ponded moist air cools to its dew point, lying thickest at dawn.

questions.question: Explain how valley climate influences the location of farming and settlement, including one planning failure and its correction.
questions.expected_answer: Frost-sensitive, high-value crops such as orchards and vineyards are planted on the thermal belt, safe from floor frost, with sun-loving crops on the warm north-facing aspect and forestry or pasture on the cooler south-facing slope; hardy crops use the fertile but cold valley floor. Farmhouses and towns historically sit on the lower slopes above frost, fog and floods, while roads follow the flat, fog-prone floor. A planning failure is placing low-cost housing on cheap valley-floor land — the coldest, foggiest, smokiest, most flood-prone zone; the correction is housing on the mid-slope, industry outside the inversion pond, and the floor kept for fields, parks and the floodplain.
